The Data Science Center grew out of UCLA's Social Science Data Archive, an archive
that dates to 1961 and was a founding member of ICPSR. Since 2017 it has become
something broader: general-purpose research data infrastructure, instruction, and
consulting used across the university. This is a record of what that build looks
like, in numbers and in the work it supported.

::: {.tldr}
**In short:** UCLA Dataverse has grown from 9 datasets in 2020 to roughly 1,390
released today. DSC's Redivis platform, built around an unusable 10-terabyte national
voter file, has since processed 4.8 petabytes of restricted research data. Workshops
have reached more than 1,600 attendees across 148 UCLA departments. GIS support
disappeared in 2024 even though the demand for it never did.
:::

Together these describe a shift: DSC has grown from a specialized archive service
into general-purpose research infrastructure used across the university, the kind of
reach the 2014 transfer was meant to enable.

## What we cover {#sec-what-we-cover}

DSC's work spans the research data lifecycle and the methods that have grown up
around it: data management and curation, data cleaning and analysis, geospatial
methods and GIS, 3D and drone-based scanning, machine learning and AI, research
software engineering, reproducible workflows, and open source and open science
practice. Consultations and workshops touch nearly every division: the largest
single workshop constituency is Geography, and social science departments together
account for about 1 in 8 attendees, but Life Sciences, Physical Sciences, Public
Health, Medicine, Humanities, and the professional schools are all steady users.

Social science departments have stayed a core constituency throughout: roughly 200
workshop participants since 2020 from Geography, Psychology, Political Science,
Sociology, Economics, Anthropology, Urban Planning, Public Policy, and Gender
Studies, plus people who registered simply as "Social Science." That share has held
steady even as DSC's overall reach grew, evidence the 2014 move broadened the
Archive's audience without leaving its original constituency behind.
